newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Malev sees '97 cargo trade up 10-15 pct.
newsitem.headline: Malev sees '97 cargo trade up 10-15 pct.

text.p: BUDAPEST, March 24 (Budapest) - Hungarian national airline Malev Rt said on Monday it expected charter flights and mail delivery to boost its cargo trade by 10-to-15 percent in 1997 from 15,278 tonnes in 1996.

"Overall, we hope to increase our volume 10-to-15 percent from last year," Ferenc Harmath, Malev's commercial manager for cargo operations, told Reuters. "Most growth will come from new business on charters and mail contracts."
Mail deliveries in 1996 soared 692 percent to 983 tonnes for exports and 529 percent to 625 tonnes for imports, he said.
"We won several mail tenders in 1996 in Belgium, Britain, Denmark, Germany, Greece, the Netherlands and Sweden," he said. "And we expect our mail volumes to grow a little bit in 1997."
Less dramatically, charter shipments in 1996 grew 390 percent to 1,045 tonnes for exports and 52 percent to 84 tonnes for imports, Harmath said.
Hungary's strong agricultural industry, providing an estimated 25 percent of the country's gross domestic product, powered Malev's growth in charter exports, Harmath added.

Malev started ad hoc flights last year to deliver farm equipment and mechanical parts to Damascus and Sana'a, the capital of Yemen, on Antonov An-124 'Coke' aircraft licensed from British charter broker Airline Charter Services (ACS), he said.
The airline also began ad hoc flights to ship day-old chickens to Mineralnye-Vody in the north Caucasus of Russia on Ilyushin Il-76 'Midas' planes licensed from ACS, Harmath said.
And Malev started ad hoc flights of hatching eggs to Algiers and Istanbul on Antonov An-12 'Cub' aircraft licensed from Bulgarian national airline Balkan Bulgarian Airlines, he said.
"We plan to continue flying these same destinations with bigger volumes this year because we have new orders," he said.

However, scheduled passenger flights, which provided 83 percent of Malev's cargo business in 1996, yielded the weakest performance for freight. Exports fell 12 percent to 3,824 tonnes, while imports rose only 18 percent to 7,193 tonnes, he said.

"Many scheduled flights use small planes like Fokker 70s and Tupolev 154s, which offer limited cargo capacity ," Harmath said. "Passenger travel has been increasing, and the extra luggage that comes with this has further reduced the available capacity for cargo."

Malev is owned 63.9 percent by the Hungarian state privatisation agency APV Rt, 30.0 percent by Italian airline Alitalia, 5.0 percent by the Italian Ministry of Foreign Trade's investment agency SIMEST and 1.1 percent by other interests, including Hungarian municipalities.
